body: Over roughly the next ninety days, you will practise becoming slower to anger. Not a different person, just a steadier version of the one you already are.
Today, notice when irritation first arrives. You do not have to change anything yet. Simply spot it.
Anger is a normal human feeling. The aim here is not to stop feeling it, but to have more say in what happens next.
Pay attention to where anger shows up in your body first. Hot face, clenched fists, a tight chest? That is your early warning.
A quick temper often grew out of real pressure or old hurts. It made some sense once, even if it costs you now.
Notice the times of day you snap most easily. Hunger, tiredness and rushing all shorten the fuse.
If you lost your temper recently, try not to pile shame on top. Shame tends to make the next flare-up more likely, not less.
Irritation is often a signal that something matters to you. It is worth listening to, even when the volume is too high.
Think of the last time you snapped. What happened in the minute before? The trigger is often smaller than the reaction.
Being calm is not the same as being a pushover. Steady people still say what they need.
Notice the small grumbles today: the slow driver, the noisy neighbour, the full sink. They add up across a day.
Anger often sits on top of other feelings, like fear, hurt or embarrassment. Ask gently what might be underneath.
You do not have to win every disagreement. Some arguments are not worth the cost to your peace.
Watch the thoughts that light the fuse, such as they always, they never, how dare they. Those words pour fuel on the fire.
The people around you may have learned to tread carefully. You can start to change that, one calmer moment at a time.
Wanting things done properly is fine. Expecting everyone to do them your way, at your speed, is where frustration grows.
Two weeks of noticing. Simply seeing your patterns more clearly is real work, and it matters.
Next time you feel heat rising, breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. A long exhale tells your body to ease off.
Try a pause phrase today, such as give me a moment. It buys you time without shutting the other person out.
When you feel a flare, unclench your hands and drop your shoulders. Softening the body can soften the mood.
Before replying to an annoying message, wait ten minutes. Most sharp replies look different after a short walk.
Eat something before a difficult conversation. A surprising amount of temper is low blood sugar in disguise.
Try lowering your voice slightly when you feel annoyed. A quieter tone often calms both you and the person listening.
Leave five extra minutes for one journey today. Rushing is one of the quickest routes to snapping.
When someone frustrates you, try imagining one ordinary reason they might be acting that way. Tired, distracted, worried?
Go for a brisk walk after a stressful moment. Moving helps the body burn off the charge that anger leaves behind.
Write down what is bothering you before you say it out loud. Seeing it on paper often shrinks it to its real size.
Try saying I feel frustrated instead of you always. It invites a conversation rather than a counter-attack.
If an argument is heating up, it is fine to say you need a break and will come back to it. Then do come back.
Notice your jaw right now. Many people carry tension there all day without knowing. Let it loosen.
A month in. Is there one situation where you reacted a little more slowly than you used to? Give yourself credit.
Choose one small daily irritation and decide in advance how you would like to respond to it next time.
Try counting the things that went right today, not just the ones that grated. Your mind tends to collect the grievances.
Ask a question before you react: what did you mean by that? Misunderstandings cause a lot of needless heat.
Get to bed a little earlier tonight. A rested mind has much more patience to draw on.
Practise letting one small thing go completely today. Not swallowing it, just genuinely deciding it does not matter.
Splash cold water on your face or hold something cool when you feel a flare. A change in temperature can reset you.
Notice when you are holding a grudge from earlier in the day. It may be leaking into conversations that have nothing to do with it.
When you feel annoyed with yourself, speak to yourself as you would to a friend having a rough day.
Name the feeling quietly: this is irritation. Naming it puts a little space between you and it.
Try sitting in silence for three minutes today. Steadiness is easier to find when you have practised it in calm moments.
If you snapped yesterday, a simple apology helps. You do not need to grovel, just own it and move on.
Look for patterns in your flare-ups: same person, same place, same topic? Patterns can be planned for.
Agree a signal with someone close to you that means I am getting heated, let us pause. Plans made in calm help in heat.
Turn down background noise when you can. A constant racket wears down patience without you noticing.
Halfway. Think about which practice has helped you cool down fastest. Keep it close at hand.
Notice the difference between a response and a reaction. A response has a breath in it.
Before a meeting or family gathering you dread, take two minutes to picture yourself staying steady through it.
Try being curious instead of certain. I wonder why they did that leads somewhere different from they did that on purpose.
Spend time doing something that drains off stress, such as exercise, music, a hobby. A full tank tips over more easily.
When traffic or queues test you, use them as practice. Every red light is a small chance to rehearse patience.
Notice how calm people move. Slower hands, softer voices, longer pauses. You can borrow some of that.
If you are frustrated with a device or object, step away rather than force it. Things rarely improve when shouted at.
Try listening to the end of someone's sentence before forming your reply. Interrupting often fuels heat on both sides.
Let someone else be wrong about something minor today without correcting them. Notice how that feels.
Think of a moment you stayed calm when you might once have exploded. Remember how it felt afterwards.
Steadiness is a muscle. Each time you pause before reacting, it gets a little stronger.
When you feel criticised, try saying thanks, I will think about that. You can decide later whether it was fair.
Look after the basics this week: food, water, sleep, fresh air. Patience runs on them more than we realise.
Notice what kind of mood you bring into a room. You have more influence over the atmosphere than you might think.
You are becoming someone who takes a breath before they speak. People around you can feel that difference.
More often now, irritation comes and passes without taking the wheel. That is real, hard-won change.
You are turning into a person others feel safe to bring problems to. Calm makes you easier to talk to.
A bad day with a short fuse does not undo your progress. It is one day, and tomorrow you can begin again.
When stress piles up, the old temper may return. Expect it, forgive it, and use the tools you have built.
You are becoming someone who can disagree firmly without raising their voice. That is a strength, not a softness.
Notice how much less energy you spend being cross. That energy is now free for things you actually care about.
If you flare up, ask afterwards what pushed you over: tiredness, hurt, fear? Understanding it is how you prepare.
You are learning to trust yourself in tense moments. That trust grows each time you stay steady.
You are someone who repairs quickly after friction. Saying sorry and starting again is a mature skill.
Certain people and places may still test you. It is fine to plan ahead or limit your time with them.
Your calm is becoming something people can rely on. That is a quiet gift to the people you love.
Holidays, deadlines and family events can stretch anyone. Go easy on yourself, and lean on your steadying habits.
You are becoming the kind of person who lets small things stay small.
Notice the peace that comes from not carrying every annoyance with you. Light shoulders are a good sign.
Anger is no longer running the show. You feel it, you listen to it, and you choose what to do.
Old reactions may still flicker. A flicker is not a fire, and you know how to let it die down.
You are someone who chooses words carefully when it matters. That care shows in your relationships.
If someone tries to provoke you, you can decline the invitation. Their heat does not have to become yours.
You have become better at spotting the moment before you react. That moment is where all the change happens.
You may feel lighter, more patient, more at ease. Let that remind you why this was worth doing.
You are becoming steady enough to stay present in hard conversations without needing to win them.
Look back at the start of this series. Which flash points that once caught you every time barely register now?
Pick the two or three calming habits that worked best for you and keep them going. Simple tools last longest.
Write a few lines to your future self about what staying calm has given you. Read it on a difficult day.
New frustrations will come along. You now know how to notice the heat rising and give yourself room to choose.
Being slower to anger is not about never feeling it. It is about meeting it with patience, and you can do that.
Notice how your relationships feel now compared with the start. Calmer moments leave room for warmth.
Be proud of the patience you have practised. Changing an old reaction takes real courage and persistence.
Keep asking yourself a simple question when things heat up: what would the steady version of me do now?
You have shown yourself that a quick temper can slow down. That knowledge is yours to keep.
This is the last note in this series. Keep taking that breath before you answer. Steadiness suits you.
